‒ i voted in favour of the cadec report because i believe that fraudulent labelling of fishery products is not only a violation of eu rules, in particular the common fisheries policy, but also misleads consumers, jeopardises their food security and the stability of marine resources and also distorts the internal market. i believe that european consumers can have full confidence in the entire supply chain of fishery products in the european market and that the eu and the member states have a duty to protect their citizens against fraudulent acts. the outcome of several studies indicating significant levels of mislabelling of fish products sold on the eu market is regrettable. i would stress the call on member states to strengthen national controls in an effort to combat fraud to identify the stage in the supply chain where fish is incorrectly labelled, and to take measures to improve the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products from landing to consumption.
‒ the people's republic of china is one of the largest economies in the world and europe has a major trade relationship with this country: china is now the second largest trading partner of the european union; the european union is china's largest trading partner. total trade between the two economies is running at one billion a day and foreign direct investment between them has been growing significantly. the european union has set out five criteria for determining whether or not we are in a market economy. according to the latest assessment by the european union, china meets only one of the criteria. indeed, 56 of the current 73 anti-dumping measures imposed by the european union concern imports of chinese goods. china does not meet all these criteria and therefore its market economy treatment should be rejected for the time being. the change in its status should only take place when the european union considers that china fulfils all the criteria set.
‒ at the time of china's accession to the wto, a specific methodology for dumping calculation was provided for, which was included in section 15 of the accession protocol, in which china committed, inter alia, to allow all its prices to be determined by market relations, and the eu should ensure that china fully complies with its wto obligations. in this regard, the commission should coordinate with the eu's main trading partners on how best to ensure that all provisions of section 15 of the protocol of accession of china to the wto remain in force after 2016. in parallel, as long as china does not meet the five criteria set by the eu to be considered a market economy, the eu should use the exceptional methodology in the anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations concerning chinese imports. i therefore agree that the eu should undertake a general reform of the eu's trade defence instruments, with the aim of ensuring that its industry is on a level playing field with china and other trading partners, in full compliance with wto rules.
‒ as long as china does not meet the five criteria imposed by the eu to be considered a market economy, an 'exceptional methodology' should be used in relation to chinese imports. it is noted that 56 of the 73 anti-dumping measures currently in force in the eu concern imports from china. any decision on how to deal with chinese imports must ensure that european law is in line with wto rules. i further agree that china's overcapacity is already having important social, economic and environmental consequences in the eu and, even in terms of employment in the eu, the social effects of granting china market economy status could be substantial.
‒ this is an issue that goes far beyond the trade issue, which is inseparable from the complex process of rearranging forces at the global level, from china's role in this process and from the relations between the transatlantic bloc and china. the eu has linked five criteria to the definition of the concept of a 'market economy'. china currently meets one of those criteria. we do not accept either the preponderance of the concept in the definition of the rules (or the absence of rules) governing international trade, or the criteria which the eu has decided to attach to it. we are in favour of regulated trade in the interests of the people, not unregulated trade, which tends to lower living and working conditions - the aim of the wto. we believe that each country should determine its trade policy in a sovereign manner in accordance with its own specific interests. the whole logic of the argument in this resolution treats the impacts of trade with china as if the eu were a homogeneous bloc. it's not a good idea. on the other hand, the eu institutions are given the power to decide on the level of trade relations, which is an attack on the sovereignty of the member states, which are held hostage to commitments that they do not negotiate and that go against the national interest, as is the case in portugal.
‒ china is one of the eu's most important trading partners and for trade relations between the eu. i have followed the line of the european parliament's motion for a resolution which refuses to grant china market economy status. the eu has imposed five technical criteria for the definition of a market economy and china currently meets only one of these criteria. preliminary estimates show that around 188,000 jobs could be lost in eu sectors currently affected by chinese dumping if no mitigation measures are taken.
‒ china is a strategic trading partner for the european union, being its second largest trading partner, generating a turnover of over eur 1 billion per day. the chinese state joined the world trade organisation in 2005 and committed itself to allow all prices to be determined by market conditions, and the eu should ensure that china complies with this obligation. however, there has been state influence in the economy, distorting the signals reflecting supply and demand. i therefore vote in favour of the joint resolution signed by the epp group, because i believe that china must respect its obligations as a member of the wto.
in writing. ‒ from the point of view of trade relations, the question is whether or not they continue to place barriers on a wto member country. in this context, it should be stressed that, from the point of view of the eu's integration process, what we are witnessing is the imposition of its federalist character and of its great economic power. the whole logic of the argument treats the impacts of trade with china as if the european union were a homogeneous bloc, and gives the european institutions the power to decide the level of trade relations, which is an attack on the sovereignty of the member states who are held hostage to commitments that they did not negotiate and that go against the national interest. the resolution even says that the commission should coordinate this issue with the eu's main trading partners, particularly in the context of the upcoming g7 and g20 summits. member states, such as portugal, must be able to define their economic strategies and establish trade relations with other countries. the country's grip on this issue, for example because of the eu's common market strategy, is unacceptable, since it is unable to take measures to provide special protections for the national economy and production. i therefore abstain.
‒ aggressive pricing practices lead to adverse effects on the economies of importing countries. in order to prevent material injury from such practices, legal safeguards are necessary to allow for differential treatment of imports from countries whose economies do not meet the five relevant criteria for market economy status (mes). since 2001, the provisions of section 15 of the protocol of accession of china to the world trade organisation (wto) have provided the legal basis for the application of an exceptional methodology to imports from this part. in accordance with the accession protocol, the suspension of the decision to award the mag by the european union effectively expires on 11 december 2016. parliament also called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the eu's trade policy is not distorted by the threat of a trade war, and to ensure that the eu's trade policy is not distorted by the threat of a trade war. in view of the above, and in order to ensure that eu industry has a level playing field with china and other trading partners, i voted in favour.
‒ it establishes the importance of the partnership with china, in which fair and free trade plays an important role. it stresses that china is not a market economy and that the five criteria set by the european union to define market economies have not yet been met. this vote is a significant sign that parliament will not accept any measures which weaken our ability to defend against abusive and unfair practices. the commission needs to take into account the concerns expressed by industrialists, trade unions and other bodies about the consequences for eu jobs, the environment and also sustainable growth in all the sectors affected. it called on the council to reach agreement with parliament on the modernisation of its trade defence instruments against chinese dumping.
in the case of the joint resolution we adopted today, of which i am one of the proponents, i would just like to highlight a few ideas. the first is the fact that china is not a market economy and will not be until the end of the year. secondly, that the european union will respect the rules of the world trade organisation in its trade relations with china. thirdly, we will have to undertake a thorough reform of our trade defence mechanisms to ensure appropriate levels of fair competition between our companies and our trading partners. the mechanisms for establishing producer prices in comparative terms and for launching anti-dumping or anti-subsidy investigations should follow a specific framework from 11 december, the date on which the current system expires. after this house's support for these positions, we now expect the commission to come forward with credible and workable proposals with regard to our trade relations with china (after the public consultation process is completed). i remember that we do not have much time left to act proactively and haste, as we know, is the enemy of good decisions.
‒ china has established itself as a strong player on the international scene and as one of the eu's main trading partners. with the approaching expiry of article 15 of the world trade organisation (wto) protocol in december 2016, the eu has to adjust its trade defence mechanisms in bilateral trade with china. it is necessary to assess the potential consequences of granting market economy status to china for the european economic and social sector. the implications will be felt in terms of industrial employment, investment and competitiveness. when china joined the wto in 2001, it committed to implementing reforms towards a market economy. however, after 15 years it meets only one of the five criteria that it should meet to be considered a market economy. i voted in favour of the resolution because i believe that granting china market economy status will have serious economic consequences for the eu, in particular for the development of a sustainable economy, for the metal and chemical industries and for jobs in the eu.
‒ we are sensitive to the profound impact that such recognition will have on our productive apparatus. and this position stems from past experiences with the opening of the eu market to global competition in key sectors of the portuguese economy such as textiles or footwear. it is not clear why the parties which are now so concerned about the chinese market have not shown as much concern in the past about opening up the eu market to countries such as india or pakistan, to name just a few. this question also raises the question of the role of the european union, which is now unilaterally exercising the right to decide what is or is not a national economy. he wants to teach lessons in democracy and now also in liberal economics. in other words, as we have pointed out, free trade agreements are not neutral and often become instruments of political interference.
‒ i voted against the recognition of china's market economy status because i consider that china does not yet meet the criteria necessary to be considered a market economy. i would point out that given the current level of state influence in the chinese economy, the decisions of companies in terms of prices, costs, production and factors of production do not respond to market signals reflecting supply and demand. i would also remind you that in its accession protocol china has committed itself, inter alia, to allow all its prices to be determined by market forces and that the eu must ensure that china fully complies with its wto obligations. i submit that, as long as china does not meet the market economy criteria, the european union should use an exceptional methodology in the anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigations concerning chinese imports to determine price comparability.
‒ following the adoption by the united nations in september 2015 of a new strategy for the 2030 agenda for development through the adoption of 17 sustainable development goals, the un general assembly called for the objectives and targets to be monitored and reviewed on the basis of a set of global indicators, and the progress report should support the monitoring and review work of the high level political forum on sustainable development. i support this resolution because i believe that the new universal framework for sustainable development requires greater coherence between the various eu policy areas and actors, through greater eu coordination, in order to ensure the integration of the environmental, economic and social pillars into the eu's internal and external policies, and that the foreign affairs council should, before the july meeting of the development forum, adopt a coherent and common eu position, taking into account the position of the european parliament.
‒ the proposed set of 230 indicators for the sustainable development goals (sdgs) represents a good starting point and provides a solid framework for monitoring and assessing progress towards the 17 sdgs. i therefore agree that the foreign affairs council should take a coherent and common eu position, taking into account the position of parliament as expressed in this resolution. the 2030 agenda and the sdgs represent a renewed international commitment to eradicate poverty, redefine and modernise our development strategies for the next 15 years and ensure that we deliver.
‒ the '2030 agenda for sustainable development' consists of 17 objectives, divided into 169 targets. adopted unanimously in september 2015 at a un summit, the 17 sustainable development goals, modeled after the millennium development goals, are intended to be a shared vision for humanity and a social contract with the peoples of the world. the resolution not only welcomes the objectives and the importance of their universality, but also highlights the fact that the eu (as a regional bloc) and its member states (individually) have committed themselves to implementing all the objectives and targets. however, throughout the resolution there is no criticism that the eu's own formal and informal legislation (notably on economic governance) is an obstacle to the achievement of these objectives, as the institutionalization and imposition of neoliberal policies have further aggravated poverty and hunger, deregulated labour laws and therefore have de-dignified work, accentuated class inequalities, degraded public health and education services and inhibited economic growth. while we are aware of the urgent need to work towards achieving the sdgs, we cannot remain indifferent to the eu's hypocrisy and its omission in this resolution.
‒ i supported the european parliament's motion for a resolution calling on the european commission to come forward with a proposal for a comprehensive sustainable development strategy covering all relevant areas of domestic and foreign policy, with a detailed timetable up to 2030, including a mid-term review and a specific procedure ensuring the involvement of the european parliament. i voted in favour.
‒ i understand that the high level political forum (hlpf) has a key role in reviewing the implementation of the sustainable development goals (sdgs) and that it should ensure a coordinated and effective needs assessment and the adoption of the roadmaps needed for the effective implementation of the 2030 agenda. the 2030 agenda and the sdgs represent an international agreement with the aim of eradicating poverty, redefining and modernising our development strategies for the next 15 years and ensuring that we achieve results. i believe that the eu should adopt a sustainable development strategy and its implementation policies should be the subject of a broad consultation involving all stakeholders, including national parliaments, local authorities and civil society.
‒ the '2030 agenda for sustainable development', adopted in 2015 at the un, consists of 17 goals based on the millennium development goals. they are meant to be a common vision for humanity and a social contract between world leaders and the people. the resolution not only welcomes the objectives and the importance of their universality, but also highlights the fact that the eu (as a regional bloc) and its member states (individually) have committed themselves to implementing all the objectives and targets. however, throughout the resolution there is no criticism that the eu's own formal and informal legislation (notably on economic governance) is an obstacle to the achievement of these objectives, as the institutionalization and imposition of economic and neoliberal policies have further aggravated poverty and hunger, deregulated labour laws and therefore have de-dignified work, accentuated class inequalities, degraded public health and education services and inhibited economic growth. while we are aware of the urgent need to work towards achieving the sdgs, we cannot remain indifferent to the eu's hypocrisy and its omission in this resolution. for this reason, we abstained.

in writing. ‒ i am absolutely in solidarity with the 2030 agenda and the 17 sustainable development goals (sdgs). i think it is very important that there is a commission communication on the follow-up and review of the 2030 agenda which contains clear information on the structure of the implementation of the agenda at union and member state level. i also believe that the budget proposals and implementation of the european institutions should reflect respect for the sdgs and that member states' budgets should allocate specific funds to achieve the sdgs. since all these perspectives are reflected in this motion for a resolution, i voted in favour. i am in general agreement with amendment no 1. however, i consider it excessive to be certain that the international trade agreements in preparation will have negative impacts on the sdgs and it seems to me that we should not scatter this important document over other legal initiatives that are under way. that's why i abstained.
‒ at a time when the un and governments around the world continue to shout the sustainable development goals (sdgs), it is important to clarify that they do not represent the interests of the majority of the world's population - those who are exploited and oppressed under the current political and economic order. the sdgs say that we can eradicate poverty in all its forms by 2030. but they rely mostly on global economic growth to accomplish this enormous task. if that growth is similar to the growth of the last few decades, it will take 100 years to end poverty, not the 15 years that the sdgs promise. and even if that were possible on a shorter timetable, it would require a 12-fold increase in the size of the global economy, which, in addition to making our planet uninhabitable, will obliterate any progress against poverty. instead of hiding this obvious folly with false hopes, we must begin by addressing two crucial problems: income inequality and the economic system that generates this inequality.

‒ one of the main concerns of european citizens has been the question of the origin and provenance of certain foodstuffs such as meat, milk and milk products, whether for reasons of public health or for the right to information for an informed consumer choice. i support this resolution, which strengthens labelling and consumer information on foodstuffs, and special attention should be paid to the origin of meat in processed foods in order to ensure greater transparency throughout the food chain and restore consumer confidence.
‒ 84% of european citizens think it is necessary to indicate the origin of milk and 88% think it is necessary to indicate the origin of meat. the indication of the country of origin or place of provenance should be compulsory for all types of milk for consumption, dairy products and meat products, because this is a way of restoring consumer confidence in the wake of the horse meat scandal and other cases of food fraud. the extension of this obligation to other foods consisting of a single ingredient or with a predominant ingredient should be considered.
in writing. ‒ according to article 26 (5) of regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, the commission should present by december 2014 reports and possible legislative proposals on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain types of meat and for milk, unprocessed foods, single ingredient products and ingredients representing more than 50% of a food. on 20 may 2015, the commission published two impact assessment reports, 6 months behind schedule. the conclusions in both reports were the same: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the labelling of all these categories of food remains on a voluntary basis. this resolution takes the opposite view. the commission's analysis overlooks the positive aspects of country of origin labelling, such as the benefits of greater consumer information and involvement, support for local production and economy, shorter transport distances, shorter supply chains and fresher products. the indication of the country of origin is not a panacea, but is positive from several points of view. any requirements that the measure may impose on certain smes should be duly considered in the legislative process. we voted in favour.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the compulsory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance of certain foods, because i share the view that the compulsory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance of meat in processed foods should also become compulsory for other types of meat, in addition to beef, pork, sheep, goat and poultry meat, for drinking milk and milk used as an ingredient in dairy products and for unprocessed foods, products consisting of a single ingredient and those ingredients representing more than 50% of a food.
‒ according to the 2013 eurobarometer survey, 84% of eu citizens consider it necessary to indicate the origin of milk, whether it is sold as such or used as an ingredient in dairy products. according to the same survey, 88% of eu citizens consider it necessary to indicate the origin of meat other than beef, pork, sheep, goat and poultry. i am in favour of mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance of meat in processed foods, and it should also become mandatory for other types of meat than beef, pork, sheep, goat and poultry meat, for drinking milk and milk used as an ingredient in dairy products and for unprocessed foods, products consisting of a single ingredient and ingredients representing more than 50% of a food. my favourable position is also due to the demands expressed by the azorean milk producers and the meat producers of mainland portugal, and i am thus following their concerns and demands.
in the light of the recent developments in the field of the protection of the environment, parliament called on the commission to take the necessary steps to ensure that the protection of the environment is not jeopardised by the introduction of new technologies. we also ask the commission to consider extending this obligation to other single-ingredient or predominantly single-ingredient foods by drawing up legislative proposals on these matters. the aim is to ensure greater transparency throughout the food chain and to provide european consumers with more complete information. according to a eurobarometer survey, the vast majority of consumers want to know the origin of these products.
in the case of the european parliament, the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right of initiative in the matter of the protection of the environment. in fact, according to the eurobarometer and a commission report on the subject, a fairly significant number of european consumers consider it important to indicate the origin of the product used in its unprocessed form or as an ingredient in processed food products: 84% for milk, 88% for meat and more than 90% for processed food products containing meat. it seems to me clear that only by implementing measures of this kind will greater rigour and higher quality and hygiene standards in this sector be promoted, further stimulating the restoration of consumer confidence in food products and promoting greater transparency, traceability and readability of the information provided to them through labelling. in this resolution i advocated compulsory labelling for the origin of the products in question, against the recommendation of the political group to which i belong, which advocated voluntary labelling. i did so, together with the portuguese members of the ppe, for the reasons stated above.
‒ the indication of the origin of meat and milk on the label allows for differentiation which, by recognising the quality and expressing consumer preference, contributes to the enhancement of the value of the products, the territory and the agricultural employment involved. this is of particular interest when the agricultural sector, and in particular the milk sector, is experiencing a persistent price crisis. in the azores, the region from which i come, milk production is one of the main activities on which the regional economy depends and is also a striking element of the regional landscape and culture. the sector has modernised and invested in quality improvement to offer a product with superior characteristics to consumers. the designation of origin 'azores' is a way of associating the product with the quality of its production, which should be recognised and preferred by consumers. the rules underlying the labelling of origin should be strict as regards the correspondence between the mention and the content, precisely to ensure consumer confidence. i therefore support the indication of origin on the labelling of meat and milk because it is an element that allows the consumer a choice which is reflected in the defence of local and quality agricultural production.
in the light of the above, the commission considers that the proposed measures should be implemented in a manner which ensures that the products concerned are not used in the same way as those originating in the member states. the implementation of policies that guarantee fair production quotas and rights in this context and not asymmetrical production as the liberalisation of markets promoted by the eu does. policies that defend national production. secondly, the commission would have to take account of the need to ensure competitive prices for similar products of the same quality as those of foreign producers, i.e. to ensure that producers have the same working methods and access to the goods and services needed for production at similar prices and quality. in addition, proximity to and access to national production is increasingly being affected by policies that promote and support large retailers at the expense of local and traditional trade.
in the light of the recent developments in the field of food safety, the commission has decided to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: at a time when there are many examples of media coverage of processed foods with ingredients other than those indicated on the packaging, it is imperative to restore consumer confidence in labels on the one hand and the credibility of the food industry on the other. to this end, i would stress the call on the commission to submit legislative proposals to make the indication of the origin of meat compulsory in processed foods, as well as in other types of meat other than beef, pork, sheep, goat and poultrymeat, in drinking milk and milk used as an ingredient in dairy products and in unprocessed foods, single-ingredient products and ingredients representing more than 50% of a food.
‒ the importance of a balance between family life and working life is indisputable. much progress has been made in this area, including the guarantee of a set of rights for european mothers. however, there is a growing need to ensure some level of protection for paternal parents, both as protection of family life and in the wider context of promoting gender equality. portugal is an exemplary member state in this respect, guaranteeing protection for both. there are, however, many member states where this is not the case. it is clear that there are still gaps that need to be addressed, in particular in the transposition of the applicable directive. there are also considerable differences between the various member states, but the increasing mobility of european citizens makes the benefit of approximating the various legal systems clear. while recognising that social benefits are a matter for the member states, i believe that issues such as the payment of paternity leave or the defence of more simplified schemes, removing unnecessary barriers to these social rights, should be points of consensus at european level.
‒ fathers and mothers do not take parental leave in the same way, which is detrimental to families and the situation of women in particular, who often end up sacrificing their career prospects in favour of their children. there is a directive in the eu aimed at countering this trend, but the results of its implementation have been mixed. in the eu, workers are entitled to parental leave when a child is born or adopted. however, in europe, access to and remuneration for this leave is determined by national legislation, which varies significantly between member states. i agree that paid parental leave is essential to ensure that men take it because it allows a better balance of the various spheres of life between men and women, ending discrimination at work for women.

‒ i voted in favour of the report on the framework agreement on parental leave. i believe that the european union is facing a major demographic challenge, with declining birth rates in most member states. the political debate should be centred on joint action to strengthen the role of parents by promoting work-life balance. there should be a concern to achieve greater coordination, coherence and accessibility of licensing schemes in the different member states.
‒ i am voting in favour of this directive which aims to overcome the challenges of work-life balance by allowing the family to reconcile their personal and professional lives. it is also important to stress that mothers who have unfortunately had premature babies should have greater flexibility and longer parental leave in order to accompany their children on the spot and whenever necessary. finally, i would like to stress the importance of the political debate also focusing on a series of non-legislative initiatives with a view to joint action with the member states and civil society in order to enhance the role of parents and promote work-life balance.
‒ the document fails to analyse the actual causes of the decline in birth rates or the deepening of inequalities. it omits the inseparable link between the increasing deterioration of workers' living and working conditions, the destruction of public services and facilities and the neoliberal and austerity policies imposed by the eu. the report does, however, list some policy proposals that we are supporting:- the need to review legislation to improve on issues such as duration, payment, transfer and scope;- the reinstatement of the maternity leave directive;- the call for women to be guaranteed the right to combine work with rights and the right to maternity without being penalised for doing so;- the importance of extending the scope of the right to parental leave;- the extension of the minimum duration of parental leave from four to at least six months. it should go further, in particular in the allocation of parental leave allowances paid at 100% of reference pay, alongside the need for wage increases and labour rights as a way of promoting maternity rights. it is a positive document in general and justifies a vote in favour.
‒ i recall that the framework agreement on initial parental leave between the social partners' organisations, which later became the council directive, dates back to 1996 and was completely revised in 2010. the aim of this report was to assess their implementation, which often varies considerably between member states (duration, legal form, etc.). it also links up with motherhood and fatherhood, since they often overlap, and makes a number of proposals for improving and modernising legislation. some of the proposals are: gender equality in the sharing of family responsibilities and an increase in the rate of participation of fathers in parental leave; an increase in the participation of women in the labour market (target of 75% in europe 2020, currently at 63.5%); the promotion of work-life balance; an increase in the age of the child for whom parental leave can be taken; improving coordination, coherence and accessibility with regard to national leave systems, ensuring non-discrimination, including here entry and return to the labour market.
‒ the purpose of this report was to assess the application of parental leave legislation by the different member states. unfortunately, there are wide differences in the way parental leave is applied in the different member states. in order to respond to the enormous demographic challenges we face, the challenges of economic growth and the need to promote gender equality in the union, this report warns of the need to correct these differences. it is considered that this legislation should be revised in order to strengthen the points concerning the duration, remuneration, coherence, transferability and scope of the licences. i would like to say that i agree with the principles proposed in general, but i would point out that this is a matter in which the principle of subsidiarity applies and that it is the responsibility of the member states to define their national policies on the family. so, although i voted in favour of the final report, i would point out that many of the proposals in the original proposal have been amended and i have voted in line with the ppe voting list, except for the granting of special leave for the support of premature babies - (proposal for a) measure which i supported - and the extension of the period of parental leave (on which i abstained).
‒ the report lists some concerns and draws a number of policy conclusions, many of them positive. it falls short of what we advocate, in particular the absence of a reference to 100% pay, the emphasis on increasing wages and labour rights as a way of promoting the rights to maternity and a happy childhood in a context of gender equality, the extension of compulsory time for mothers and fathers and full transferability in the remaining period. however, in view of the above, it is considered to be a positive document and therefore deserves a favourable vote.
‒ the fight against trafficking in human beings is an absolute priority for the european union. a scourge that knows no borders and which has unfortunately become even more worrying with the so-called 'refugee crisis'. but the union, and this is largely thanks to the european parliament, is not only concerned with the scale of the fight and the repression, but also with prevention and with providing the greatest possible support to those who are victims of this crime. the directive in this area has already been transposed by 27 member states. it is clear that everyone should apply it, but it is also important to ensure that it is transposed correctly. on the other hand, as the rapporteur acknowledges, there is still a lot of work to be done. in the field of prevention, member states should make use of all the means at their disposal, including europol. at the level of victims, particular attention should be paid to those most affected - women - and to the most vulnerable, such as children. i therefore support this report.
‒ trafficking in human beings is a violation of fundamental human rights as well as a violation of the personal integrity of the victim and a serious form of organised crime that undermines the state and the rule of law. a 2011 directive established a legal framework to facilitate criminal prosecutions against traffickers and was recognised as a comprehensive legal instrument with a commendable human rights-centred approach and a clear emphasis on the gender dimension of trafficking in human beings. so far, 26 member states have officially notified the commission of transposition, with only germany missing. i also believe that adequate services and fair treatment of victims also play a role in prevention.
in writing. the directive on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims aims to better protect victims of trafficking in human beings and to reduce the vulnerability of potential victims. the report identifies that trafficking in human beings is driven by the pursuit of high profits, estimated at around $150 million/year. it analyses the root causes of trafficking and finds that trafficking of women, girls, men and boys for sexual exploitation has decreased in countries that criminalise solicitation, including both pimping and clientelism. it stresses that the victims are overwhelmingly women. notes that despite the directive, victims still struggle with access to justice, information, access to specialised services, including access to safe short- and long-term accommodation, witness protection schemes, healthcare, including the right to terminate a pregnancy, counselling, translation and interpretation services, judicial redress, compensation, access to education, language instruction in their country of residence, assistance with employment, (re) integration, family mediation and resettlement. despite the positive aspects, there are controversial aspects from which we distance ourselves (europol, eurojust, frontex and cepol, among others).
in writing. ‒ in the light of article 5 (3) of the charter of fundamental rights of the eu, trafficking in human beings constitutes a serious violation of fundamental rights, as well as a violation of the human dignity and physical and mental integrity of victims, responsible for serious harm to them throughout their lives. i would point out that directive 2011/36/eu should have been transposed into the national legislation of the member states by 6 april 2013 and that all member states except one have notified the commission of the transposition of that directive into national law. i believe it is essential that member states speed up the correct and full implementation of directive 2011/36/eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims. i agree with the rapporteur's recommendation that the gender dimension should be properly accompanied in the implementation of eu legislation and that member states should adopt gender-differentiated measures. men and women, as well as girls and boys, are differently vulnerable and trafficked for different purposes and that prevention, assistance and support measures should therefore be gender-sensitive.
‒ directive 2011/36/eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims of trafficking from a gender perspective aims to better protect victims of trafficking in human beings and reduce the vulnerability of potential victims. the report identifies that trafficking in human beings is driven by the pursuit of high profits, estimated at around $150 million/year. it analyses the root causes of trafficking and finds that trafficking of women, girls, men and boys for sexual exploitation has decreased in countries that criminalise solicitation, including both pimping and clientelism. stresses that the victims are overwhelmingly women, victims who can be found in both legal and illegal activities, including: prostitution, agriculture, the food industry, domestic work, the manufacturing sector, the care sector, cleaning, begging, crime, forced marriage, the sexual exploitation of children online, illegal adoptions and human organ trafficking. despite an adequate overall assessment, issues such as the framework for the response centred on structures such as europol, eurojust or frontex; the proposal for an independent national rapporteur; with which we disagree, justify abstention.
‒ the report on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims from a gender perspective defines trafficking in human beings as a violation of human dignity, the physical and mental integrity of victims. this form of crime is based on the exploitation of victims which includes exploitation for the purposes of prostitution, for forced labour such as begging, slavery, exploitation of criminal activities as well as organ harvesting in order to obtain very high profits. the report warns that trafficking in human beings is taking on a gender dimension, for example 80% of victims exposed to sexual exploitation are women and girls. it also stresses the importance of protecting and identifying victims belonging to socially vulnerable groups, such as children, young people, lgbti people and people with disabilities, who are still somewhat overlooked. i voted in favour because the report calls on member states to correctly transpose directive 2011/36/eu on trafficking in human beings, further strengthens the rights of the most vulnerable, encourages greater coordination in the collection of data to identify victims and promotes exchanges of best practices to address the specific needs of such victims.
‒ directive 2011/36 / eu on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting victims aims to better protect victims of trafficking in human beings and reduce the vulnerability of potential victims. the report identifies that trafficking in human beings is driven by the pursuit of high profits, estimated at around $150 million/year. it analyses the root causes of trafficking and finds that trafficking of women, girls, men and boys for sexual exploitation has decreased in countries that criminalise solicitation, including both pimping and clientelism. the report clearly identifies that women and girls are particularly vulnerable, as well as asylum seekers, refugees and migrants, and therefore special attention should be paid to trafficking in women, children and other vulnerable groups. it urges the eu member states to provide appropriate training for all those involved in this process.

in writing. on 16 december, the european commission was condemned for failing to propose a definition of endocrine disruptors. this definition is, however, essential for a regulation. these molecules, which are found in many plant and food products, are the cause of many health problems. it was the commission's duty to protect the health of europeans; it has chosen to defend the interests of the industrial lobbies. in response to this failure, a motion of censure against the commission was tabled and unfortunately failed. only this motion was likely to put pressure on the commission. but instead, we are offered a resolution, without binding force. it's an attempt to smoke. it is for those who have not asked for censorship to make europeans believe that they care about public health. the patriots will not participate in this charade. this resolution is a bad communication operation for the gullible. meanwhile, nothing is being done to protect the health of europeans.
the court of justice of the eu found that the european commission had infringed community law by failing to meet the deadline for publication of marketing standards for chemicals harmful to health, such as bisphenol a, pesticides or solvents. the court's ruling does not include a fine but requires that the document on scientific criteria for determining the harmfulness of so-called endocrine disruptors be adopted as soon as possible. the decision stems from the case brought by sweden against the commission, which should have adopted the standards by the end of 2013. two years too late, as denounced by several european associations, which speak of a public health problem, when endocrine disruptors will be the cause of various diseases such as cancer or even increased infertility. this is yet another sign of the interests these institutions are defending.

member of the commission. – madam president, i’d like to start by thanking the rapporteur, ms arena, for her report on gender inequality in the world of work and on the implications that this has for our society. i would also like to thank her for setting out the recommendations in the report so clearly. while the female employment rate has increased to just above 64% in 2015, women’s lower earnings and under—representation in the labour market continues to mean that their financial situation is less secure than men’s. as we heard, many more women than men are living in poverty in the eu and – as she explained – the risk of poverty is especially high among single mothers, and also among older women. women’s lower pay and the fact that they often do part—time work and take gaps in their careers often leads to gender pension gaps; women’s pensions are 40% lower than men’s and, of course, women are less likely to have a pension at all. in june last year, the council agreed some conclusions on the gender pension gap, and these called for work to continue to narrow this gap, and for member states’ social and employment policies to be assessed as part of the european semester process. last december, the commission published a strategic engagement for gender equality that set out the overall framework for european initiatives that were aimed at improving gender equality and, in that, priority areas included increasing the numbers of women in work, reducing the gender pay gap and the pension gap, and also making women more financially independent. we continue to keep a close eye on these issues and we have provided country specific recommendations to those that face the greatest challenges. as set out in your report, adequate work—life balance policies are needed so that women who want to can play a full part in the labour market. last year, the commission launched a ‘new start’ initiative to improve work—life balance for parents and other people caring for family members. that looks at a range of measures to promote adequate leave and flexible working arrangements and to support affordable professional care services. the second phase of the consultation will be launched shortly, on the legislative parts of the ‘new start’ initiative, and my colleagues will be tabling proposals on that by the end of the year. the commission’s plans to create a european pillar of social rights have gender equality also at their heart. the draft pillar that’s now been agreed for wider consultation puts the emphasis on improving the situation of women in the labour market. i think that fairness, which lies at the heart of this report, is central to the commission’s agenda, and the principle that no one should be left behind will continue to drive forward our work to support greater gender equality in europe.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating mrs comi on her report. it is an important contribution to the improvement of the single market. it sets out a set of measures vital for a stronger, fairer, consumer-centred market for the 21st century. i would remind you, as the commissioner has already done, that, alongside schengen, the single market is one of the greatest achievements of the european union, which european citizens feel in their daily lives and which has completely transformed the way we trade, consume and move around within the european area. the potential of this market of over 500 million consumers is not fully exploited. potential efficiency gains of €615 billion are estimated from further integration of the single market. however, obstacles to the free movement of goods and services persist, such as unjustified non-tariff regulatory requirements and several member states not applying part of the important legislation in force. there is also a persistent distrust of cross-border contracts by consumers and some digital illiteracy. all this represents unnecessary waste to the real economy and hinders further growth and job creation. i therefore welcome the results achieved, in particular the emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises, the strong investment in market digitalisation and the fight against geo-blocking, the optimisation of the single digital portal, the initiatives in the sharing economy and the improvements in public procurement. finally, i would stress the urgency of the product safety and market surveillance package, which is blocked in the council, and the urgency for member states to ensure the proper application of the services directive.
‒ virtual currencies represent a technology with undeniable potential, but which lacks further elaboration, and does not yet guarantee that it can be considered a currency with all its prerogatives. the report is balanced and seeks to avoid giving a false message of total reassurance to potential users of this new instrument. since the concept of the blockchain was created, many currencies have been created and many have died. many more are yet to be born. others were forced to close down for providing cover for illegal activities. we are still living in a period of uncertainty. doubts remain about the limited or even finite nature of the money supply, at least in the current form of mining. there are lingering doubts about his still very volatile character. the report, in essence, adequately reflects these doubts and limitations of virtual currencies. it points out shortcomings and recognises the need to monitor this phenomenon, which is already attracting the interest of major economic groups. we voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology can make a positive contribution to citizens' well-being and economic development, particularly in the financial sector. it is therefore necessary to strengthen regulatory capacity, including technical capacity, and to develop a robust legal framework that keeps pace with innovation, ensuring a timely and proportionate response if and when the use of some applications of distributed ledger technology becomes systemically important. that is why i am voting in favour.
‒ the technology of virtual currency is booming. i recognise the hypothetical benefits of virtual currencies for the economy, including increased speed and efficiency and reduced costs when making payments and transfers, in particular internationally, and their potential to promote financial inclusion and facilitate access to finance and financial resources for the business sector and smes. however, virtual currencies may carry risks related to criminal activities such as terrorist financing, money laundering and tax fraud and evasion, among others. it is important to highlight that holders of virtual currency are vulnerable to illegal activities and challenges such as fraud, theft of virtual currency, cybercrime, computer piracy, software/hardware malfunctions, fraudulent systems and fraud, false claims or misrepresentation, and it is vital to ensure an adequate level of protection and redress for consumers who may encounter certain risks associated with the use of virtual currencies. i am voting in favour of this report which calls for the creation of a working group to study the advantages, disadvantages and vulnerabilities of virtual currencies in order to ensure consumer protection, transparency and confidence in their use and in the financial system.

‒ the use of virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology is now having a significant impact on the financial sector. those instruments contribute to citizens' well-being and economic development, in particular by reducing transaction costs and protecting users' privacy. however, virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology present risks, such as legal uncertainty and high volatility associated with their use, the propensity for the formation of speculative bubbles and the potential to stimulate the shadow economy and criminal activities. the use of distributed ledger technology outside the payments and financial sector is further exacerbating these contingencies. in my view, the report on virtual currencies provides an appropriate response to these risks by advocating the strengthening of smart regulation and the development of a sound and proportionate legal framework, and by promoting the creation of a working group with a budget, staff and skills to increase the benefits and prevent the risks of using distributed ledger technology. i therefore vote in favour of the report.
‒ the main opportunities of virtual currencies are related to reduced transaction costs and ease of use, while providing resilience and varying levels of privacy protection. many of the potential of this technology is likely to extend beyond the payments sector. however, virtual currencies and the underlying ledger technology carry risks that will only become clearer as their use becomes more widespread. some of those risks have already become apparent, for example the misuse of certain applications for criminal activities, including money laundering and terrorist financing. the smooth functioning and resilience of these systems must be ensured on the basis of sound governance and oversight structures. in addition, consumer protection issues are likely to be relevant in a number of applications. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment.
‒ this own-initiative report on virtual currency and distributed ledger technology - a technique for organizing digital records into blocks, cryptographically and chronologically linked in a chain, using complex mathematical algorithms, in which all transactions are recorded - at all nodes in the network. this new technique will allow any banking transaction to be recorded in a decentralised manner, while maintaining the privacy/security of the data and preventing its alteration or tampering. it also has the advantage of being made by anyone, anywhere in the world, without a minimum/maximum value limit or intermediaries. nevertheless, there are some risks associated with virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology, namely phishing, as well as the possibility of money laundering or terrorist financing. this is why it is important to ensure functional and efficient regulatory structures and effective monitoring/supervision mechanisms. overall, i consider this to be a good first report on this subject, the implementation of which could bring benefits to consumers, businesses and the economy in general, contributing to the improvement of money transfers and thus contributing positively to the development of the digital single market, and i therefore voted in favour of this report.

‒ i support the jäätteenmäki report which will allow the use of eur 58 146,800 from the globalisation adjustment fund to reintegrate into the labour market 2 132 workers made redundant by moryglobal sas. these redundancies are associated with the general decline in physical production in europe, which has resulted in a decrease in the volumes transported and a price war in the road transport sector, causing a steady reduction in operating margins and a series of losses for the sector in france since 2007, followed by a wave of bankruptcies. through the use of this fund, which was set up to provide complementary support to workers due to major structural changes in world trade, it will be possible to support these workers through measures ranging from guidance/interpretation and facilitation of job search to support for business creation or personalised vocational retraining.
in writing. ‒ mory-ducros was the second largest operator in the land transport and pipeline transport sector in france, operating between 4 and 500 vehicles per day. from 2008, road transport by vehicles weighing more than 3,5 tonnes decreased in the eu and france. the bank of france estimates that the number of bankruptcies in the sector increased by 35% per year between 2007 and 2013. the bankruptcy of mory-ducros was declared in november 2013. the liquidation procedures have been initiated. arcole industries, the main shareholder, an investment company specialising in companies in difficulty, submitted a bid for the acquisition of mory-ducros, submitting a 'social plan' for its employees. a new company was created, mory-global, which took over part of the mory-ducros business and rehired only half of the workers, despite many talks with the unions and the french government. the unions continued their struggle and 200 workers were reinstated. the liquidation of mory-global was declared in early 2015. however, the court noted that the shareholder appeared to have lost interest in the mory-global restructuring project and its sustainability. the unions are accusing arcole industries of willful underinvestment. what a shame. capitalism in all its glory.
‒ the eu is an area of solidarity and the european globalisation adjustment fund is part of it. these supports are essential to help the unemployed and the victims of displacement in a globalised context. the number of companies relocating is increasing, taking advantage of the low labour costs in several countries, notably china and india, with harmful effects for countries which respect workers' rights. the egf is intended to help workers who are victims of the relocation of companies and is essential to facilitate access to a new job. the egf has been used in the past by other eu countries and this aid should now be granted to france, which submitted an application for a financial contribution from the egf, following redundancies in the whole of metropolitan france in the economic sector classified under nace revision 2 division 49 (land transport and transport by pipeline) and division 52 (storage and transport auxiliary activities), where it is expected that 2 132 redundant workers eligible for the egf will participate in the measures. that is why i am voting in favour.
in writing. regulation no 1927/2006 of the european parliament and of the council of 20 december 2006 established the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) to support workers who have lost their jobs as a result of structural changes in the global economy. the application of france for the egf relates to the mobilisation of a total of € 6 052 200 of the financial contribution from the egf, following redundancies in the economic sector classified under nace revision 2 division 49 (land transport and transport by pipeline) and division 52 (storage and transport auxiliary activities) in metropolitan france, where it is expected that 2132 redundant workers eligible for the egf will participate in the measures. i support the mobilisation of this financial envelope to cover the shortfalls in the road freight transport sector. this situation is also due, among other things, to the global economic and financial crisis which caused road freight transport to decline in european economic activity by 13,7% and in the particular case of france by 21% between 2007 and 2012 (eurostat).

in writing. ‒ on 8 december, sweden formally requested the suspension of its obligations under council decisions (eu) 2015/1523 and (eu) 2015/1601 due to the fact that it is facing an emergency situation characterised by a sudden influx of third-country nationals into its territory following a sharp change in migratory flows. the considerable increase in irregular border crossings into the european union, and secondary movements across europe, has led to a sharp increase in the number of applicants for international protection in sweden, most of whom entered the eu via italy and greece. sweden registered the highest number of applicants for international protection per capita in the eu in 2015 (11 503 applications per million inhabitants). this situation has put pressure on the swedish asylum system, with serious practical consequences on the ground, in terms of reception conditions and the capacity of the asylum system to deal with these applications. i shall vote in favour of this report because of what it says and because it is designed to ensure that sweden has the support it needs to deal with this emergency situation.

in writing. these motions for resolutions follow the decision of the court of justice of the eu of 6 october 2015 which declared the european commission decision 2000/520/ec, known as the safe harbor agreement, invalid on the grounds that it had clear implications for changing the rules on the transfer of personal data from the eu to the us. in a context where negotiations are under way on transatlantic free trade agreements (for example, ttip and tisa), the issue of data transfer is all the more important as rights such as the privacy of citizens are at stake, but also the commercialisation of data and the internal security of states. these motions for resolutions put the handling of this issue on a supranational level, between the european commission and the united states of america, subordinating the member states and, with that, the imperative need to deal with this issue sovereignly and democratically in each country, in accordance with its legitimate interests. the resolutions do not address a wide range of concerns regarding the protection of personal data. the amendments tabled by our group were partly intended to fill these gaps. unfortunately, they were rejected. that is why we are voting against it.
‒ protecting data means protecting the persons to whom the information processed relates, and such protection is one of the fundamental rights recognised by the union (article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights and article 16 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union). the protection of personal data, respect for private life and communications, the right to security, the right to receive and impart information and the freedom to set up and manage businesses are fundamental rights that must be respected and balanced. the eu-us privacy shield agreement should be consistent with eu primary and secondary law and with the relevant judgments of the european court of justice and the european court of human rights. that is why i am voting in favour.
‒ in view of the development of the information society and electronic commerce, there has been an exponential increase in the circulation of electronic data and communications, as well as in the risks associated with the misuse of such data and the interception of such communications. these abuses not only hinder the development of electronic commerce by undermining consumer confidence, but also constitute a violation of the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals. i am voting in favour of this report because i agree with the views expressed on the efforts made by the commission and the us administration to achieve substantial improvements under the privacy shield compared to the safe harbor decision. however, i cannot but express concern that the privacy shield agreement may not fully comply with the requirements of the charter, the directive, the general data protection regulation and the judgments of the court of justice and the european court of human rights in this area. despite the importance of transatlantic trade and cooperation, of legal certainty for data subjects and data controllers, i believe that safeguarding fundamental rights, including the rights to data protection and privacy, is fundamental.

in writing. the increasing volume of data and electronic communications, a natural corollary of today's information society, underlines the relevance of the transatlantic relations established between the us and the eu. the report on transatlantic data flows states that in the context of the abovementioned relationships, it is important to safeguard the right of consumers to the protection of their data, enshrined in the fundamental rights recognised by the union in articles 8 of the charter of fundamental rights and 16 of the tfeu. i therefore believe that the protection of citizens' data should be ensured not only within the european economic area but also in third countries to which data are transferred, in accordance with directive 95/46/ec. in this particular case, relations between the us and the eu generate the largest flow of data in the world, and legal certainty in the transfer of this data is therefore of the utmost importance to guaranteeing consumer confidence, the development of transatlantic business and cooperation between the judicial forces of these two western powers. it is precisely because this is a report which stresses the need to improve the us-eu privacy shield, without prejudice to the urgent need to promote transatlantic relations, that i am voting in favour of its adoption.
‒ this resolution highlights the importance of transatlantic cooperation in the field of data transfer, but also underlines the need to safeguard fundamental rights, including the right to data protection and privacy. the commission has also identified a number of concerns regarding the complexity of the redress mechanism for individuals under the privacy shield; the insufficient penalty measures for possible violations; the lack of change in the legal situation regarding mass surveillance by us agencies outside the us and of foreigners inside the us; the lack of an assessment by the commission of the rights of eu citizens when their data is transferred by a us data controller to us law enforcement agencies.
