in writing. ‒ since 2005, eu listed companies are required to prepare their consolidated financial statements in accordance with international accounting standards. these standards form an important part of the eu regulatory and supervisory framework for financial services. however, the financial crisis has demonstrated that international financial reporting standards need to be reviewed and improved. in particular, the consequences of the use of the notion of 'fair value' on financial stability have opened a debate which is still ongoing.
‒ the report provides an assessment of the international accounting standards (ias) of the international financial reporting standards foundation (ifrs), the advisory group on financial reporting in europe (efrag) and the public interest oversight board (piob). it is part of the assessment of the working group on accounting standards, also targeting the activity of the institutions which define them, and recommends reforms in the definition of these standards. ias play a key role in the eu's financial regulatory and supervisory services. the question of convergence of international standards in this context does not raise major problems in an internationalised commercial context. however, the framework of these specific rules raises some issues, which the report does not always address critically, such as: their need in the context of the internal market and the capital market; the need to strengthen democratic legitimacy, transparency, accountability and public access to documents, public dialogue between stakeholders and the prevention of conflicts of interest; or the transformation of efrag into a public agency. the report has some positive points, but it is not critical of the internal market and the single capital market, which gives it a negative framework.
‒ international financial reporting standards (ifrs) and international auditing standards (isa) are fundamental elements for the effective functioning of the internal market and capital markets and can be seen as a public good and thus should not compromise financial stability or harm the economic development of the union, and should serve the common good and not only the interest of investors, lenders and creditors. i argue that international accounting standards are a key part of the eu regulatory and supervisory framework for financial services, interacting with a wide variety of acts of eu regulation on financial services, including in the field of prudential regulation. it is important to emphasise that the falsification of company accounts is a threat to economic and financial stability and calls into question citizens' confidence in the social market economy model. i agree with the rapporteur in recognising the importance of such globally applicable standards in improving competitiveness and removing barriers to investment on a global scale.
‒ this report addresses the need to review and improve international accounting standards (ias), both in terms of the regulatory framework and in addressing issues relating to the adoption process of international financial reporting standards (ifrs) in the european union. the ias board is currently developing a set of high quality, globally applicable accounting standards by creating a common language for the financial lexicon worldwide. and this is where it becomes necessary to strike a balance between the complexity inherent in including financial reporting in accounting standards with the requirement to make them more transparent and understandable to users and other stakeholders. the principle of proportionality should be respected in the application of ias, which should be uniform, consistent and adapted to market-traded companies, growing smes and smaller companies wishing to be listed on a stock exchange. the aim being to evaluate the current accounting standards and to standardise eu financial services, making them more transparent, rigorous and effective and, above all, to increase european involvement and influence at all stages of the legislative process at global level, i voted in favour.
‒ international accounting standards are an important part of the eu's regulatory and supervisory framework for financial services. these rules interact with a wide range of eu regulatory acts on financial services, in particular in the field of prudential regulation. we follow the report on the central role of accounting standards in developing a more transparent and more readable market for the community. what we don't follow is this association of the need to improve international accounting standards with the current financial crisis. international accounting standards are important, but they cannot replace the fundamental measures required to control the world of finance, preventing this unregulated and unbridled speculation which leads to crises whose costs are ultimately borne by the same people as always. that way, we don't confuse the plans for the intervention. the crisis will be resolved when there is the political will to take the necessary measures. they are subject to public control of the financial system and of the large oligopolies that are currently in power in the european union.
‒ un peacekeeping operations are one of the most important instruments of the un. the un's collaboration with the african union should be supported by the european union and this report contains important recommendations for more effective implementation of this support. i would like to stress the need for coordination between the various actors in order to avoid overlapping actions and to better manage the resources allocated. the united nations has the largest peacekeeping force in the world, the vast majority of which is in africa. the european union contributes more than 35% of these forces and, as the report says, it is important that member states are willing to significantly increase their contributions in order to improve investment in conflict prevention. for these reasons i shall vote in favour of this report.
‒ peace support operations (psos) are a form of crisis response, seeking to prevent armed conflict, restore, maintain or consolidate peace, ensure compliance with peace agreements, and respond to emergencies and complex challenges associated with failing or fragile states. unfortunately, the security situation, especially in africa, has changed profoundly over the last decade due to the emergence of terrorist and rebel groups in somalia, nigeria and the sael and sahara region. the main mechanism for european cooperation with the african union (au) is the african peace facility, originally established in 2004, which provides some eur 1.9 billion through the european development fund (edf). this report, which i have supported, highlights the need to invest more in conflict prevention, taking into account factors such as political and religious radicalisation, electoral violence, population displacement and climate change. i stress that support for border management must be a priority of eu intervention in africa. the porosity of borders is one of the main factors in the rise of terrorism in africa.
‒ peace support operations are a form of crisis response and aim to prevent armed conflict, restore, maintain or consolidate peace, ensure compliance with peace agreements and respond to emergencies and complex challenges associated with failing or fragile states. 16 un peacekeeping missions are under way, with over 120 000 peacekeepers deployed, an unprecedented number, with 87% of un peacekeeping personnel assigned to eight missions in africa. i believe that the crises in africa require a comprehensive and coherent response, which must go beyond purely security aspects, and i agree with the need for coordinated external action using instruments in the fields of diplomacy, security and development in order to restore confidence and respond to the challenges posed by wars, internal conflicts, insecurity, fragility and transition processes.
‒ this report focuses on peace support operations in africa, addressing the eu's engagement with the un and the african union. it does so without disguising a certain neo-colonialist and militarist stance, rather than seeking to contribute to the effective guarantee of peace on the continent under the auspices of the un. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union. the commission is also proposing that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft budget for the european union for the financial year 2000 and that the council should be consulted on the draft budget for the european union for the financial year 2000 and that the council should be consulted on the draft budget for the european union for the financial year 2000. in other words, those who already have a colonial past in the countries in question. as you would expect, the role of the eu (and nato) in destabilizing the region is hidden. a role always justified by the defence of human rights, but whose real motives go beyond the control of important natural resources and wealth of these countries. the report advocates the financing of military operations through the european development fund. we obviously voted against it.
‒ peace support operations (psos) are a crisis response instrument and aim to prevent armed conflict, restore or consolidate peace, ensure compliance with peace agreements and respond to emergencies and challenges associated with fragile states. it is important to stress that peace and security are indispensable preconditions for development and i advocate the need for coordinated external action using instruments in the fields of diplomacy, security and development in order to restore confidence and respond to the challenges posed by wars, internal conflicts, insecurity, fragility and transition processes. the change in the security situation in africa due to the emergence of terrorist and rebel groups in somalia, nigeria, the sael and the sahara cannot be overlooked. i support the need for coordinated external action using mechanisms in the fields of diplomacy, security and development, with the aim of restoring confidence and responding to the challenges posed by wars, internal conflicts, insecurity, fragility and transition processes, bearing in mind that the stability of the african and european neighbourhood would be extremely beneficial for all.
‒ the report addresses the issue of peace support operations in africa and the eu's commitment to the un and the african union. it treats these peace operations from a neo-colonialist and militarist perspective and not from the perspective of contributing to the effective guarantee of peace on the continent under the auspices of the un and with respect for the sovereignty of the african states. it calls for a greater military and police contribution from the member states to the region. he advocates greater collaboration between the un, the eu and nato and faster forms of intervention in these african countries, proposing the leadership of the coordination of the intervening countries in a neocolonialist vision. this report conceals the role of eu member states in destabilising the region, as well as the growing influence of nato. interventions which are almost always justified by the defence of human rights, but whose main objective is always to control the geostrategic position and the important natural resources and wealth of these countries. we voted against it.
‒ the presentation of coordinated strategies to respond to crises in africa, particularly in the fields of diplomacy, security and development, is crucial. this obviously requires early communication and strengthened consultation procedures in crisis situations with organisations such as the un, the au, nato and the osce. there is a need to improve the exchange of information, including on the planning, execution and analysis of missions. in an increasingly complex security context, un and au missions require a global approach. we must invest more in preventing conflicts rather than just in remedying them.
‒ the un is the main actor in the difficult task of ensuring international peace and security, with the vast majority of its efforts concentrated in africa. this report focuses on the eu-un strategic partnership for peacekeeping and crisis management and its priorities for 2015-2018. the eu and its member states contribute approximately 37% of the budget for un peacekeeping programmes. in africa, the eu is contributing through the african peace support (aps) programme, whose action plan has identified perceived shortcomings and emphasised strategies for resolution. the apa constitutes an important starting point with the potential to create a strengthened partnership between the eu and the african union. in addition to military and police contributions to un peacekeeping operations, i believe that the eu should continue to lead the operationalization of forces in africa, including the exchange of intelligence, information and technology services or training and logistical support. i think it is important that the eu and the un continue their efforts and support for the empowerment of africa to become self-sufficient on its own territory, and i therefore voted in favour of this report.
‒ the report on peace support operations (pso) aims to prevent armed conflict, consolidate peace and respond to complex challenges linked to rogue states. africa has been facing an unprecedented wave of instability over the past few years, imposed by terrorist and rebel groups in somalia, nigeria and the sahel. the emergence of fragile states and regions without a consistent form of government, which do not meet the necessary conditions to guarantee the prevalence of fundamental rights and the prosperity of their population, condemning it to extreme poverty, anarchy and violence, also undeniably endangers the security and stability of third states. in this context, there appears to be an urgent need to improve the performance of the african union and the african regional communities as a means for the success of the plo and the rehabilitation of post-conflict countries. i voted in favour of the view that the eu has a relevant role to play in the context of the plo, continuing to provide financial and technical support to the african union and subregional organisations as a means of intensifying the fight against violence in africa, thus contributing to development, good governance and respect for human rights.
‒ contrary to the prophecies of the 1990s that heralded an era of peace, security and prosperity, we live today in a more dangerous world, with more wars and more inequality and misery. these wars, almost always disguised as humanitarian intentions, reflect the need of the rich countries to dominate the large reserves of raw materials. to do this, they encourage corruption. africa is tired of meddling. it is tired of corrupt governments supported by multinationals with the connivance of capitalist countries. it is tired of the successive manoeuvres of interference in which arms are poured into the continent and fratricidal wars are fomented to the satisfaction of the large multinationals of the military industrial complex. africa is crying out for a new paradigm in international relations. a paradigm based on respect for national sovereignty, respect for self-determination, the right of each people to dispose of its resources and to choose its own model of development.
‒ unfair trading practices can have negative consequences for actors in the food supply chain, especially farmers and smes, which in turn can have an impact on the entire european economy and on final consumers, limiting their choice of products and their access to new and innovative products. these practices occur most often where there are inequalities in trading relationships between partners in the food supply chain resulting from disparities in bargaining power and are a real obstacle to the development and smooth functioning of the internal market, disrupting its functioning. despite the existence of voluntary self-regulatory and national regulation schemes, some problems tend to persist. i support the czesak report because i think it is important that the commission presents a uniform european framework to combat pcds throughout the food supply chain, encourages member states to create or recognise public services/agencies that implement the application of control and sanctioning measures, and focuses on consumer information on agricultural products, imbalances in the chain and certification systems that allow informed product choices and action.
the report calls on the commission to put forward one or more proposals to combat unfair trading practices in the food supply chain, in order to ensure transparent relations between producers, suppliers and distributors. i also express my concern about food waste, the sale of food below cost of production and the misuse of certain agricultural products - milk, fruit and vegetables - as 'balance products' by large retailers. these practices can have negative consequences for actors in the food supply chain, especially farmers and smes, which in turn can have an impact on the european economy and on final consumers, limiting their choice and access to new and innovative products.
in writing. ‒ in 2014, the european commission published a communication calling on member states to look at ways to protect small producers and retailers in the food sector against unfair trading practices (utps), which occur whenever one party is in a stronger position than the other in a trade relationship. it was no good. the negotiating power of agricultural producers and agro-industries is gradually being lost to the power of large retailers. dumping between member states is a common practice, influencing the level of prices along the value chain from primary production through processing to the final consumer. the imbalances between member states with different production systems at different stages of development are becoming more pronounced, leading to growing deficits and greater food dependency in countries with weaker production systems. the option has been to avoid the issue of abuses by 'big buyers' in the food supply chain. not to disturb the current concentration of power in the hands of retailers and large industries, nor to propose measures to sustain and reverse this situation. the european commission merely issues communications in which it undertakes to introduce mechanisms to combat these diseases by encouraging the adoption of voluntary codes of conduct. nothing changes now.
‒ i have tabled my vote in favour of the motion for a resolution on unfair trading practices in the food supply chain. the fight against unfair trading practices in the food supply chain is essential to ensure transparent relations between producers, suppliers and distributors. the big retailers must respect the farmers and producers. it is not fair that producers should see their agricultural products sold below the cost of production, such as milk, fruit and vegetables. in the long term, if nothing is done to tackle unfair trading practices, we will put the future of eu production of these products at risk, with huge losses for farmers and smes.
‒ unfair trading practices in the food supply chain seriously harm small producers by making the relationships between small producers, suppliers and distribution less clear and transparent. that is why i am in favour of a regulatory framework that protects producers and smes against these unfair practices, namely selling below production costs, thus jeopardising the long-term sustainability of production. on the other hand, these practices may also have the effect of reducing the available products and increasing their prices. for the reasons set out above, i am voting in favour of this report.
‒ this report only gives examples of unfair trading practices that food supply chain actors have declared to be common in the sector. we believe that a clear, rigorous and objective definition of abusive and unfair practices is necessary. the value chain is a major issue in the food supply chain. the prices paid by consumers for products do not reflect the prices paid to producers, which are often overwhelmed by the imposition of the distribution sector, particularly by the large retailers, guaranteeing them absurd profit margins, while producers are often charged prices below the cost of production. the commission has chosen not to address the issue of abuses by 'big buyers' in the food supply chain. instead of strongly opposing the current concentration of power in the hands of retailers and large industries and proposing measures to sustain and reverse this situation and promote an active fight against dumping, it merely issues communications in which it commits itself to introducing mechanisms to combat these unfair trading practices, encouraging the adoption of voluntary codes of conduct and at the same time creating eu-wide standards for the principles of 'good practice'.
in writing. the report under review addresses the issue of unfair competition practices (ucps) and acknowledges the efforts already made by the member states and the union in this field. the issue of pcds in the context of inter-company relations has gained ground in recent years and the subsequent debate has been supported by statistical data. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted through state resources and does not distort competition and affects trade between member states. these practices result in a loss of investment and innovation capacity of firms and therefore damage the eu economy. the consequences of dpcs are now recognised by a large number of member states and their legal frameworks include a number of measures to regulate certain aspects of these practices. the report, however, takes the view that the community context lacks a specific regime, in particular a clear definition of the pcds and the provision of sanctions for those who use them. for these reasons, and because i consider it essential to establish a trade regime of its own for the union, i voted in favour.
‒ unfair commercial practices (ucps) are those which significantly deviate from good commercial conduct and are imposed unilaterally by one trading partner on the other (contract changes, late payment, restricted market access, forced price reduction). they may have detrimental effects on the eu economy, as they may result in a loss of investment and innovation capacity of enterprises, in particular smes. many of these smes are also reluctant to take legal action against stronger companies for fear that the commercial relationship will be jeopardised. in a survey conducted in march 2011, 96% of respondents in the food supply chain said they had been exposed to at least one form of pcd. the rules in this area differ considerably from one member state to another, as does the scale of the problem. the fact that dcps are a widespread and growing problem calls into question the effectiveness of self-regulatory regimes in restoring market balance. rules at eu level are needed to ensure that markets function properly and that there are fair and transparent relationships between all parties involved in the food supply chain.
in writing. ‒ we are seeing today situations that can constitute unfair trading practices in the food supply chain, fostering non-transparent relationships between producers and wholesalers/retailers. we also see huge food waste, reports of sales below the cost of production and the misuse of certain agricultural products - milk, fruit and agricultural products, for example, sold at very low prices in promotions. all of this should make us think and act. i therefore supported the adoption of this report, which calls on the commission to put forward proposals to combat these practices, in order to bring about greater transparency, clarity and rigour in the relations between the food production and marketing sectors. we shall thus be contributing to an overall reduction in costs and an increase in revenues for firms with less bargaining power, as well as to facilitating the disposal of their production and, consequently, to reducing food waste, thus leading to more responsible consumption. in the absence of effective voluntary and self-regulatory schemes, concerted action at european level is needed to pool efforts and provide european farmers and consumers with a level playing field in all member states.
‒ farmers are currently suffering from crushing prices which, in some sectors such as milk, are at historically low levels. in addition to unfavourable market conditions, the relationship of farmers with industry and distribution reveals differences in terms of bargaining power, which results in lower prices for farmers. the need to ensure the disposal of their products often forces farmers to accept conditions which force them to revise their yield forecasts downwards. european legislation is urgently needed to rebalance this relationship and guarantee a fair price to farmers. this is particularly important in regions whose production depends heavily on distribution to sell their products, such as the azores.
‒ large-scale distribution is now a central problem affecting the whole food production sector in a widespread way. the criticisms come from all sides and they all coincide in a reality that is terrible. the large distribution network, by virtue of its weight, now absorbs the lion's share of the value added along the entire production chain. in other words, it lives at the expense of those who produce, by crushing the prices paid to producers and by imposing improper margins which are an insult to the thousands of farmers who close their businesses every day because of a lack of profitability. the proposed measures are only a palliative. the eu, which is so quick to attack nation states and democratically elected governments, does not seem to be very motivated to intervene on this issue, which is pointed out by the majority of economic actors as one of the main obstacles to the survival of broad economic sectors, notably the agricultural and food sectors.
in writing. ‒ food demand is expected to grow by 70% by 2050. the reduction of available land, environmental loss and degradation, the scarcity of water resources, the increasing demand for energy and the emergence of new pests and diseases are putting considerable pressure on our environment. technological innovation is a key part of the solution. the eu must take global leadership in agricultural technology, innovation and sustainability. finding solutions that work on a small scale in rural communities is equally important to tackling the challenges faced by many of our large farmers.
‒ this report assumes that technological innovation is a key part of the solution to the reduction of available land, environmental degradation, water scarcity, increasing demand for energy and the emergence of new pests and diseases. however, it tends to ignore the concrete framework - economic, social, political - of technological innovation and the application of its products. the central concern in this report is to ensure that the eu takes the global lead in technology and innovation (with more or less flourishing concerns about 'agricultural sustainability'). the whole report shows the growing pressure to create a regulatory framework that facilitates the application of new technological solutions in agriculture, otherwise, it is considered, the european agricultural sector will move to 'more dynamic markets', which is how it is said, with the ttip coming, the agricultural sector will either further deregulate or the big producers and the big distributors will flee to the usa. it regrets the restrictions that european legislation 'imposes on products and technologies without solid evidence of risks' (affecting gmos, herbicides, etc.), thus ruling out any application of the precautionary principle. it is business that must prevail over the protection of the health of the population and the environment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on technological solutions for sustainable agriculture in the eu. by 2050, the world's population is expected to reach 9.6 billion, and food demand will increase by 70 percent. we must know how to respond to this reality. this requires more and better investment in agricultural technology as well as in reducing the environmental impact of agriculture.
‒ the increase in the world population, the satisfaction of the demand for healthy food and optimal nutrition, as well as the reduction of available land, environmental loss and degradation, the scarcity of water resources, the increasing demand for energy and the emergence of pests and diseases are putting considerable pressure on our environment. these are the big challenges ahead. technological innovation is a key part of the solution, and agricultural technologies have the potential to make agriculture more productive and sustainable. this report aims to ensure that europe has an agricultural sector capable of developing a wide range of technologies and innovations for all types of agriculture. it is important to stress that rural areas, in particular the outermost and mountainous regions, are more vulnerable to climate change, with the risk of depopulation and ageing of the population, and consequently of abandonment of all agricultural activity. i believe that the challenges of sustainable agriculture must be met with a common strategy of the commission and the member states to ensure support for technological innovation, a risk-based and scientifically-based regulatory framework, the continuity of basic research and the development of agricultural skills.
‒ the report under consideration highlights the challenges in the areas of agricultural production in the context of an increasing world population and in line with the requirements of optimal nutrition and the demand for healthy food. the rapporteur argues that europe must optimise its production, including in the agricultural sector, in order to ensure the sustainability of resources and to make the most of technological innovation. to this end, taking the lead in world technology, innovation and agricultural sustainability, while ensuring that all european farmers have access to the benefits of technological developments, is of crucial importance. on the other hand, europe lacks human capital and technical know-how in the fields of agronomy and plant pathology, and it is therefore clear that the sustainability of agriculture in europe requires bringing farmers and scientists closer together in order to improve the practical translation of research and foster a new phase of agricultural innovation. i therefore voted in favour.
‒ i voted in favour of this resolution on technological solutions for sustainable agriculture in the eu, which aims to draw attention to the increasing difficulty of producing food in a balanced and sustainable way, given the scarcity of available (fertile) land and water resources, as well as the increasing degradation of our environment. the proposed solution proposes to make use of the technological innovations we have in the agricultural sector, making it more innovative, competitive and sustainable in the long term. it is also important that the use of these new technologies in agricultural production can also be of service to the vast majority of the people in developing countries who are hostages to chronic malnutrition and malnutrition. the new horizon 2020 framework programme could provide a window of opportunity for funding in the area of agricultural research and innovation. a new, more simplified and innovation-friendly regulatory framework will also be key to achieving a more modern and globally competitive european agricultural sector. only concerted work between the eu institutions, member states, academia and the agricultural sector will develop cutting-edge technological solutions for a truly sustainable and competitive agriculture, enabling europe to move to a new phase of agricultural innovation.
‒ innovation should be at the service of all types of farms, including those of the most modest or family size, for which the outermost regions can be a good laboratory. innovative solutions can contribute to more resource-efficient agriculture and improve the competitiveness of farmers. the text we are discussing includes references to new breeding techniques. i understand that we cannot take an obscurantist position on these, because we must and have the obligation to create an environment conducive to the development of science, but always, and i repeat, always, with powerful and very precautionary precautions as regards the impact on the environment and on the health of animals and people. more debate and more information are needed if we are not to take too much for granted. we must not impede the development and work of research centres in these areas, but we must be very cautious in the transition to production and consumption.
‒ the report contains positive and relevant aspects. but it's not real. and the reality is that today in the western world, we produce too much food, we pay to eliminate food products. the technology applied to agriculture today has become a problem that will only end with a new economic model of production and distribution. technology is now driving intensive production which is endangering biodiversity and the balance of our planet. the gmos and glyphosate, which the commission has decided to extend for a further seven years, are the most illustrious offspring of this technology. we do not deny the need for further research into agricultural practices. but first we have to understand each other. agriculture subject to the laws of capitalism and the maximum accumulation of profit can only give rise to ever more intensive and productivist technologies. before we talk about technology, it is therefore important to reverse our cap, which is now completely liberalized.
‒ i voted in favour of the mcintyre report because i agree with technology-based solutions for modern and sustainable agriculture in the eu. i would stress that the compilation and analysis of large integrated data sets has the potential to promote innovation in the agricultural sector and is particularly useful for addressing and developing an efficient and sustainable food chain, with benefits for farmers, the economy, consumers and the environment. i support the call on the commission and the member states to remove obstacles to the integration of complex and fragmented ict systems, by encouraging investment and supporting training costs and by making the necessary infrastructure more accessible to agriculture. i would stress that i voted against paragraphs 30 and 31 which refer to new methods of animal or plant breeding because i consider that the text does not include the due precautions which must accompany the development and use of these techniques. i would like to say, however, that the negative vote in these paragraphs was in defence of the precautionary principle and is not against the promotion of agricultural research, since i am convinced that innovation contributes constructively to the achievement of sustainable agriculture in the eu.
‒ the european agricultural sector is of central importance to the union as a whole, providing food security and at the same time being a key economic pillar providing employment for 25 million people who are directly involved in agricultural work, as well as those working in the food, retail and other complementary sectors. the common agricultural policy must focus more on farmers and encourage innovation and competitiveness. better alignment with other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, health and technology, through improved knowledge intersection, integration of resource use and better understanding of the reciprocal effects is needed to optimise their interaction and better integrate agriculture into the circular economy.
‒ the report 'has one thing on its face and another on its shoe'. it advocates reducing the environmental footprint of agriculture and supports extensive animal husbandry. i would also like to see the commission and the council agreeing on the need to encourage the recovery of animal protein by using waste from livestock production to produce animal protein feeds. the report calls for the continuous development of innovative plant breeding techniques, the development of new varieties with higher yields, higher nutritional value, better resistance to pests - i.e. a defence of gmos - while calling for the preservation of european seed banks and warning of the danger of chemical dependence of these new crop species. in the midst of some green rhetoric of concern about the loss of biodiversity and environmental protection, there is the apology for the increase in competitiveness - which has made current agricultural practices viable. while innovation and new technologies can help farmers, agriculture and the environment, it is the economic and social model in which they are embedded that largely determines the nature - positive or negative - of their effects and whether or not they serve a primary purpose - profit - that overrides others.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution on the strengthening of innovation and economic development in the future management of european agricultural holdings. by 2050, the world's population is expected to reach 9.6 billion, and food demand will increase by 70 percent. we must know how to respond to this reality. this requires more and better investment in agricultural technology and innovation. farmers have the capacity and knowledge to innovate, but they are limited by european legislation. i would like to point out that, for example, pest control with insects already exists, but european legislation still sometimes makes this innovation difficult. there is still a lot to be done in this area, but the eu is taking steps in this direction. the memorandum of understanding between the european commission and the european investment bank is extremely important for supporting agricultural projects and young farmers by providing new financing opportunities. this will make it possible to modernise farms and to support research more.

in writing. ‒ agricultural practices have changed, both structurally and in the production process, making the sector one of the most economically dynamic. the common agricultural policy, as the basic pillar of european agriculture, must focus on farmers and consumers simultaneously, without compromising policy objectives, by making innovation and competitiveness more flexible and better. since technological innovations contribute to targeted interventions, the application of precision agriculture and big data will transform agriculture and contribute to higher production using fewer resources. in addition, alignment with other industrial and technological sectors, such as chemicals, health and technology, is key to optimising and better integrating agriculture into the circular economy. technological and/or technical innovations will thus create more jobs and new income streams. the potential for innovation in agriculture has not yet been fully realised and some major difficulties have to be overcome in order to accelerate and stimulate innovation and entrepreneurship in the agricultural sector, since we are talking about a sector which provides employment for 25 million people and functions as a food reserve for our continent - and i voted in favour of it.
‒ innovation in agriculture requires sufficient investment in research and development and farmers' involvement in finding solutions and disseminating results. innovative solutions such as those encompassing precision farming should be at the service of all types of farms. they must have a cost/opportunity ratio commensurate with the financial capacity of smaller farms, such as those in more remote or outermost areas, such as the acores, where agriculture is an essential activity for local employment. agriculture, to feed the world, must adapt to the challenge of climate change and make rational use of available resources. to do this, we need innovative solutions, based on technology or a different approach to traditional practices, in a process where farmers must be the focus, as the main actors of change and the subject of appropriate training.

‒ i voted in favour of the huitema report because i believe that economic development and sustainable production are not mutually exclusive and that it is possible to modernise european farms through innovation, research and development. tomorrow's demographic challenges require adaptations in both food production and our way of consuming and disposing of food (100 million tonnes of food are wasted in the eu every year, 33% of which is generated by consumers). i stress the need to create synergies between new forms of economic development in agriculture and our consumption patterns in line with the principles of the circular economy. the role of agriculture is paramount in this respect through the prudent use of natural resources. i would also stress the potential for job creation not only in the food production sector but also in the tourism and green bioeconomy sectors, especially in a field where the eu is already the world's largest exporter of agricultural products, making the agri-food sector a key economic pillar of the union.
mr president, the choice is very clear. either europe remains an old continent on the defensive or it sets a partnership for the future with the neighbouring countries to support their development, to better manage migration and also to support refugees. the choice is so clear. of course this means a big undertaking, a big undertaking based on investments, but let me underline that investment is also jobs. many new jobs could be created for both young people in europe and in the neighbouring countries. i believe that you should use this argument of jobs – new jobs which can come from this initiative – to convince member states to put more resources into the initiative because we need more contribution from the member states. let me tell you that, so far, young people in europe understand this very well. they share this vision, they have many initiatives in this direction, and it is my pleasure to announce that very soon young people’s organisations will come forward with concrete proposals in exactly this direction.
mr president, the first point i wanted to make here, and which i think is the most important to welcome in this initiative of the commission, is in fact the understanding of structural factors. we have two fronts here, one which is the immediate front, which is to save lives, and i think that we cannot hesitate to put all the resources at our disposal to save the lives that are being lost every day in the mediterranean. this is an unwavering obligation of an organisation to the european union and the countries of the european union. but then you have to deal with the structural factor. and here i think that beyond the middle east, where there is, finally, clearly, in the case of jordan and lebanon, already the idea of pacts to move forward, the african question is fundamental. and, in particular, as a portuguese who knows well the african situation and what the flow of people will certainly be in the coming years, this will be something to be maintained for a long time and not just a short-term crisis. i think it is essential that we are able to intervene in particular in sub-saharan africa and that is why i think that the commission is indeed on the right track here and that the different countries of the european union, if they really want to open up to refugees on the one hand, but also to control this crisis on the other, must adhere to this commission plan. and so i would say that this is very good news at this stage and i congratulate the two vice-presidents on the effort they have made. it's not easy to defend this position at this time.
in writing. if we take into account that, as all the studies and estimates point out, the current wave of refugees is exponential and will tend to increase, we realize that this is the biggest civilizational challenge for europe since the end of the second world war. of course, there will always be economic migration. all human beings have the right to seek to escape poverty and to aspire to a better life. two million portuguese did so throughout the 20th century. europe must recognise that its history, its human, cultural and linguistic wealth has been shaped by migration and will continue to be so. we have to get used to thinking a little bit beyond the immediate. there is a whole range of information and pedagogical work to be done, starting with policy makers and ending with schools. in a time of accounting, we risk dehumanizing refugees: the risk of seeing them as numbers instead of human beings. it is the duty of each of us to counter the discourse of prejudice and fear and to remember that our human dignity depends on first recognizing the dignity of the other.
in writing. thousands of deaths in the mediterranean last week alone: it is clear that the council and the commission have no idea how to deal with the causes of the humanitarian crisis or with the consequences, and are betting on replicating the immoral outsourcing deal with turkey. and they continue to give business to traffickers by not opening legal and safe pathways of access, just as they stop explaining to europeans that the flows of migrants and refugees can help stop europe's ageing. and they're not even moving forward to create instruments to fund the integration of refugees and migrants. treating africa as "one-size-fits-all" is a gross mistake. a marshall plan for africa must begin by stopping the job-destroying austerity in the union itself. we need european governments to stop welcoming illicit flows of capital that kleptocratic elites steal from their people and states. they must stop supporting oppressive regimes, such as those in egypt, sudan, ethiopia, eritrea and others, who met at the valletta conference. and stop wasting the union's time on coordinated action in the cfsp and csdp frameworks to resolve conflicts, combat terrorism and organised crime, strengthen the rule of law, and promote sustainable development in africa, its neighbourhood and beyond.
mr president, commissioner, we must be clear on the essential point: we cannot confuse economic migration with refugees. and we have to fight illegal migration and human trafficking and regulate legal migration. and in the field of economic migration, as the commissioner said, it is clear that europe must be able to attract the best in the world and to promote internal mobility. a different issue is the legal and safe access of people fleeing war and seeking protection in our territory. we will prevent thousands of deaths in the mediterranean while fighting human traffickers. we'll manage the influx of people better. but let us be serious: resettlement mechanisms only achieve their purpose with numbers that are in line with reality. and they do not replace other access instruments, such as humanitarian visas. it is clear that the success of resettlement mechanisms depends on cooperation with third countries. but here too, a word of caution to navigation: more funding cannot be more frontloading, that is, facing the present with what was destined for the future. we can't go into 2017 and be faced with a new emergency because we didn't know how to hedge our expenses ahead of time. a final note on the integration policy. my country, portugal, was ranked the second best country in the world for integrating migrants in 2015. however, we know that there is still much work to be done. at european level, unfortunately, much more needs to be done.

in writing. the eu agenda for new skills and new jobs is part of the eu 2020 strategy, meeting the target of employing 75% of the working age population. that is, it is assumed that 25% of the working-age population will not be active. the eu-2020, behind the social and environmental rhetoric, is the implementation of policies that have materialized the degradation of the socioeconomic conditions of the populations, promoting labour flexibility and deregulation, the primacy of the deepening of the internal market, with the liberalizations and privatizations of even more economic sectors, the liberalization and deregulation of international trade. the new skills agenda has no other purpose and fits into this agenda. it advocates labour flexibility, the commodification of education and the trend towards early professionalization (through the connection of school to the labour market or dual education), the promotion of international competitiveness, through deregulation and the loss of rights and wages. education, vocational training and the diversification of technical skills are key factors in ensuring that workers adapt to the constant change of the present - whether in technology, communication methods or work management and organisation. but the objectives of this agenda are diverse: deregulation of work and narrowing the role of education systems.

the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european fund for strategic investments is a good one. we said then that the ratios were unrealistic, we said that this plan did not meet the needs of economic recovery, we said finally that this plan was not neutral because it has no criteria for geographical distribution, it favours the richest countries and it represents a real banquet for large companies through public-private partnerships. the current figures show that most investment is actually concentrated in the richest and most developed regions of central europe, confirming a framework of private management of energy transport infrastructure, which should be public and placed at the service of development and not at the service of the accumulation of profits for large multinational companies. portugal is currently at zero on the implementation of this plan, despite the fact that austerity policies have drastically reduced investment to the point where they no longer even cover capital depreciation, jeopardising future growth. instead of celebrating fictitious results, particularly in relation to smes, it is time to think about a real public investment plan at the level of each member state, thus ensuring social and territorial cohesion.
madam president, the european fund for strategic investments has proved in its first year of operation to be a strong incentive for investment in the european union. it is boosting confidence, growth and employment. it has already mobilised €100 billion, which is not a small sum, in 26 member states. moreover, of the €75 billion for the sme window, over €50 billion has already been mobilised, exceeding all expectations and the best of expectations. portugal, for example, has already used this sme scheme, which has enabled it to support more than 590 smes and mobilise more than €588 million. in view of these data, it is easy to predict and to argue that this fund should continue beyond the three years initially envisaged. it is also important that the eib complies with the regulation as regards additionality, as regards the selection of projects, which must take account of territorial cohesion and job creation. i would like to stress that the regulation does not set minimum amounts for the eligibility of projects. no one is obliged to apply for this fund, but member states and local authorities should be encouraged to do so, to set up regional, national and transnational investment platforms to maximise the geographical spread of investments. in addition, the advisory support platform, the iap adviser, needs to be disseminated so that the investment is known and mobilised across the european union.
madam president, when president juncker came to this house to announce his investment plan, he told us that christmas had come early. clearly, it was an exaggeration of optimism, but also, with the age we are, you can only believe in santa claus if you want to and you just have to spend a year of the investment plan to realize that it fell far short of what was announced. we do need investment in the european union, but not this kind of investment. we must break the taboo on public investment, and it must be in strategic sectors that create added value, such as the energy sector. i do not understand the added value of motorways in germany or the netherlands. there must be regional distribution, it cannot be concentrated in the same countries as always and with more investment. southern europe or eastern europe cannot be wiped off the map. it must be directed at the real european industrial fabric and not just at the multinationals. to say that small and medium-sized enterprises are enterprises of 3000 employees, mr katainen, is that true? finally, mr katainen, the miracle of multiplication has not happened, and the european commission remains in a state of denial, oblivious to reality and self-deluded. so, nothing new.
madam president, i would point out to mr katainen that he is the vice-president for growth and jobs. so let me recall the three objectives the investment plan and efsi should meet and, in fact, the crucial questions the european parliament will address to you to ensure a regular oversight. the questions are very simple. how far is efsi going in raising recovery and job creation? the second question is: how far is efsi going in promoting the transition to a new growth model, greener and making the best of the digital revolution? the third is: how far is efsi going in reducing the regional divergences? my conclusion, and my group’s conclusion, is that the commission needs to change something fundamental, first on the promotional strategy, because you need to build up investment platforms and to spread advisory hubs everywhere. secondly, we need to change the financial strategy. sooner or later you need to confront the need to raise the ceilings of the mff and, most of all, you need to create real room to invest in the national fiscal policies.
the strategic investment plan is one of the key tools for a change in the priorities of the european union, reinforcing investment, fostering growth and jobs and supporting competitive differentiation priorities such as the digital union, the energy union, industry 4.0 and the new smart grids. after one year of implementation, the results of the plan are frankly negative, not only in terms of the resources mobilised but above all in terms of the allocation made. the fund was mainly used to reinforce projects which could have continued to be financed by existing eu instruments and was channelled not mainly to countries with the greatest investment needs but to those where investment rates were already above the european average. it has therefore failed as a lever for innovation and as a promoter of cohesion. the strategy for implementing the strategic investment fund must be radically changed. it has to incorporate more innovation and more risk-taking. it has to finance projects with potential but which could not be financed through traditional instruments and to finance projects located in territories with difficulties in raising finance for reasons external to the merits of the projects.

in writing. the establishment of a commission of inquiry to investigate the scandals revealed by the panama papers was voted in favour. however, we cannot fail to point out that the recent past, with its succession of tax scandals, leads us to conclude that we are facing a structural problem and not just a cyclical one. this committee, regardless of whether it is investigating the facts about the perpetrators of these practices, whether they are consultancy firms, multinationals or national governments, should provoke a broad reflection on the deeper causes that created the conditions for these practices to be common and have become widespread in most large multinationals with the connivance of several eu member states. and these root causes are naturally associated with the deregulation of the financial system and the lifting of all restrictions on the movement of capital. it is to be hoped that these matters will not be the subject of the work of this committee. we regret that the mandate of the committee does not reflect this need. having made it possible to set up this committee, we denounce what we consider to be its limits and, in a certain sense, some of the perversity that may be associated with it: giving the impression that something is being done to change something, while in reality everything remains the same. that is what happened to the luxleaks commission.

‒ relations between the european union and the republic of palau are governed by the partnership agreement between the african, caribbean and pacific states (acp). the agreement provides for visa-free travel for eu citizens and citizens of palau to the territory of the other contracting party for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. the visa waiver applies to all categories of persons (common, diplomatic, service/official and special passport holders), regardless of the purpose of stay, except for the pursuit of a paid activity. visa-free travel is an important element in bringing the peoples of europe and the pacific closer together. the visa waiver agreement allows citizens to fully benefit from the acp-eu partnership. as on other similar occasions we voted in favour.

‒ relations between the european union and the kingdom of tonga are governed by the partnership agreement between the african, caribbean and pacific states (acp). the agreement provides for visa-free travel for citizens of the european union and citizens of tonga travelling to the territory of the other contracting party for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. the visa waiver applies to all categories of persons (common, diplomatic, service/official and special passport holders), regardless of the purpose of stay, except for the pursuit of a paid activity. visa-free travel is an important element in bringing the peoples of europe and the pacific closer together. the visa waiver agreement allows citizens to fully benefit from the acp-eu partnership. as on other similar occasions, we voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ according to council decision 2005/387/jha on the exchange of information, risk assessment and control of new psychoactive substances, the dangers of new drugs require rapid and concerted action by states at european level. when a new substance is detected, the member state should inform europol and the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction, which will also assess the risk to public health and associated crime. at the end of the procedure, they may request member states to take control or prohibition measures. although parliament's involvement is unnecessary given the purely technical content of this decision , parliament must be consulted and give its opinion. the substance had already been banned and, given its enormous toxicity and associated deaths, it is suggested that the ban should be maintained and parliament approves.
‒ the report proposes approval to subject substances to control measures provided for by law, by virtue of its obligations under the 1971 united nations convention on psychotropic substances. the psychoactive substance 1-phenyl-2-(1-pyrrolidin-1-yl) -pentan-1-one (α-pyrrolidinovalerophenone, α-pvp) is a psychomotor stimulant that was first registered in the eu in 2011. it's a derivative of the synthetic cathinone commonly referred to as a new psychoactive substance. α-pvp is a potent blocker of the norepinephrine and dopamine transporter and clinical research suggests that the effects of α-pvp will be similar to those of mdpv, methamphetamine and cocaine. once the submission to eu control measures has been approved, in accordance with decision 2005/387/jha (on the exchange of information, risk assessment and control of new psychoactive substances) of 10 may 2005, member states will have to legislate on the matter within 12 months of the decision. this implementing decision allows the authorities of the member states to take the measures deemed necessary to prevent the sale of such substances. we voted in favour.
in september 2015, following a request from the commission and 17 member states, an assessment of the risks posed by the consumption, manufacture and trafficking of the new psychoactive substance α-pvp, as well as the involvement of organised crime and the possible consequences of control measures that would be applied to that substance, was requested. since α-pvp is a potent psychostimulant, it has been detected in the 28 member states, as well as in turkey and norway, and in eight member states where α-pvp has been detected, a total of 115 deaths and 191 acute intoxications have been reported. on the basis of the conclusions of the risk assessment report, the commission considers that there are grounds for subjecting this substance to control measures across the union and that the acute toxicity of α-pvp can cause serious harm to human health. i am therefore in favour of subjecting α-pvp to control measures and criminal sanctions in accordance with their respective legislation.

‒ the 2010 hns convention establishes the strict liability of the ship owner in the case of the carriage of hydrocarbons and hazardous and noxious substances (hns) for damage arising from incidents related to the carriage of these substances on board the ship. it provides for the obligation of the owner to take out insurance to cover his liability for damage caused under the convention and a specific compensation fund to compensate all persons who suffer damage as a result of the nhs maritime transport, if those persons have not been fully and properly compensated by the ship owner or the insurer. the conclusion of the 2010 protocol to the nhs convention will ensure the uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation in the event of accidents caused by vessels carrying nhs within the eu. an international regime is more appropriate than regional solutions to ensure the uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation in the event of an accident. it is therefore in the interest of the union to have a homogeneous liability regime applicable to environmental damage caused by the transport of hns by sea.
‒ the 1996 hns convention and the 2010 protocol to the hns convention have not yet entered into force, the latter establishing the objective liability of the shipowner, in the case of the carriage of hns, for damage resulting from incidents related to this carriage. more importantly, it creates a specific compensation fund to compensate all persons who suffer damage as a result of hns' shipping, if such persons have not been fully and properly compensated by the shipowner and the insurance company. the total amount of compensation available amounts to approximately eur 310 million.
‒ the 1996 international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea is the latest of the international maritime organisation (imo) conventions governing liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of these substances, including liquefied natural gas (lng) and liquefied petroleum gas (lpg), which has not yet been ratified. the convention provides: - for the strict liability of the shipowner for damage caused by incidents; - for the obligation of the shipowner to take out insurance or other financial security to cover his liability for damage under the convention; - for the creation of a specific compensation fund to compensate all persons who have suffered damage as a result of maritime transport if they have not been fully and adequately compensated by the shipowner and the insurer. there is some discrepancy between the directive that exists in the eu for the same subject and the convention. it is considered to be in the eu's interest to have a homogeneous liability regime applicable to environmental damage caused by the transport of these substances by sea, which can only be achieved if parliament's recommendations are duly taken into account by the council and the commission. we voted in favour.
‒ i have voted in favour of the interim report on the draft council decision on the ratification and accession of the member states, in the interest of the union, to the 2010 protocol to the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea, as regards aspects related to judicial cooperation in civil matters. as stated by the rapporteur, the objective of the 2010 hns convention is to ensure accountability and to provide adequate, prompt and effective compensation for loss or damage to persons, property and the environment resulting from the transport of harmful and dangerous substances by sea, ensuring a uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation in the event of accidents within the eu. it will also ensure that sufficient funds are available to compensate victims of such accidents.
‒ the 1996 international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea is the last of the imo conventions governing liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea, including lng and lpg, which has not yet been ratified. in view of the experience gained with similar international regimes in the area of liability for damage caused by other maritime transport activities, in particular the transport of oil in oil tankers, the imo has adopted this international agreement as amended by the 2010 hns protocol. the convention includes: - the liability of the ship owner in the case of hns transport for damage arising from incidents related to its transport; - the obligation of the ship owner to take out insurance or other financial guarantee to cover its liability for damage; - the creation of a specific compensation fund to compensate all persons who suffer damage as a result of hns transport. the aim is to ratify the convention and eliminate legal conflict with community law, so as to alleviate the damage to people and communities affected by spills of these substances at sea. we voted in favour.
‒ i voted in favour of the resolution to ensure that the principle of conferring powers on the eu under article 5 (1) teu is respected and that the court of justice's established case-law that 'the choice of the legal basis for a community act must be based on objective elements which are capable of judicial review, including, in particular, the purpose and content of the act' is respected. as the proposal for a council decision aims to authorise member states to ratify or accede, on behalf of the union, to the 2010 hns protocol and subsequently to be bound by the 2010 hns convention, and as the latter covers not only cases of environmental damage (by applying the principles of preventive action and the polluter-pays principle) but also cases of non-environmental damage caused by the transport of certain substances by sea, the appropriate legal basis for the proposal is articles 100 (2), 192 (1) and 218 (6) (a) (v) tfeu.
‒ we are in the presence of a report on the same subject already dealt with in report a-0191/2016 (accession to the 2010 protocol to the hns convention), with a view to adopting uniform international rules regarding liability and compensation in the event of accidents caused by vessels carrying hns in the territory of the eu, although in this case, specifically, on the aspects related to judicial cooperation in civil matters. in this case too, it was decided to draw up an interim report with a view to requesting a more in-depth discussion on this matter with the commission and the council, in particular as regards the overlaps between the recast brussels i regulation and the 2010 hns convention, provided that the procedural rules applicable to claims for compensation and to legal actions under the convention before the courts of the states parties are at stake, and to ensure that the uniformity, integrity and effectiveness of the common eu rules are not adversely affected by any international commitments entered into by the union or its member states, as can be read in the document. i therefore voted in favour of its approval.
‒ the 1996 international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea is the latest of the international maritime organisation (imo) conventions governing liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea, including liquefied natural gas (lng) and liquefied petroleum gas (lpg), which has not yet been ratified. it is considered to be in the interest of the union as a whole to have a uniform liability regime for environmental damage caused by the transport of hns by sea, which can only be achieved if parliament's recommendations are duly taken into account by the council and the commission. the commission should therefore be able to conclude that the 2010 hns convention is not compatible with the internal market.
‒ the 2010 hns convention establishes the strict liability of the ship owner in the case of the carriage of hydrocarbons and hazardous and noxious substances (hns) for damage arising from incidents related to the carriage of these substances on board the ship. it provides for the obligation of the owner to take out insurance to cover his liability for damage caused under the convention and a specific compensation fund to compensate all persons who suffer damage as a result of the nhs maritime transport, if such persons have not been fully and properly compensated by the ship owner or the insurer. the conclusion of the 2010 protocol to the nhs convention will ensure the uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation in the event of an accident caused by vessels carrying nhs within the eu. an international regime is more appropriate than regional solutions to ensure the uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation in the event of an accident. it is therefore in the interest of the union to have a homogeneous liability regime applicable to environmental damage caused by the transport of hns by sea.
‒ the commission should ensure that the uniformity, integrity and effectiveness of the common eu rules are not adversely affected by the international commitments made by ratifying or acceding to the 2010 hns convention and take all appropriate measures to ensure that the exclusivity clause, according to which no complaint may be lodged against the owner of a ship which is not in conformity with the said convention, is fully respected by the member states which have ratified or acceded to the convention. i also agree with the elimination of the permanent coexistence of two maritime liability regimes.
‒ the 1996 international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea is the latest of the international maritime organisation (imo) conventions governing liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of these substances, including liquefied natural gas (lng) and liquefied petroleum gas (lpg), which has not yet been ratified. the convention provides: - for the strict liability of the shipowner for damage caused by incidents; - for the obligation of the shipowner to take out insurance or other financial security to cover his liability for damage under the convention; - for the creation of a specific compensation fund to compensate all persons who have suffered damage as a result of maritime transport if they have not been fully and properly compensated by the shipowner and the insurer. there is some discrepancy between the directive that exists in the eu for the same subject and the convention. it is considered to be in the eu's interest to have a homogeneous liability regime applicable to environmental damage caused by the transport of these substances by sea, which can only be achieved if parliament's recommendations are duly taken into account by the council and the commission. we also voted in favour.
‒ i have voted in favour of the interim report on the draft council decision on the ratification and accession of the member states, in the interest of the union, to the 2010 protocol to the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea, as regards aspects related to judicial cooperation in civil matters. as stated by the rapporteur, the objective of the 2010 hns convention is to ensure accountability and to provide adequate, prompt and effective compensation for loss or damage to persons, property and the environment resulting from the transport of harmful and dangerous substances by sea, ensuring a uniform application of the rules on liability and compensation in the event of accidents within the eu. it will also ensure that sufficient funds are available to compensate victims of such accidents.
‒ the international convention on liability and compensation for damage in connection with the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea (hns convention, 2010) aims to ensure that adequate, prompt and effective liability and compensation for loss of or damage to persons, property and the environment resulting from the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances by sea is provided for by the hns specific international compensation fund. i agree with the rapporteur's position on the appropriateness of an exception to the general rule of application of the recast brussels i regulation, given the very specific nature of the jurisdictional regime of the hns convention and the foreseeable legal and practical difficulties associated with the application in the union of a separate jurisdictional regime by virtue of an exception to the general application of the hns convention. i understand that the purpose of this interim report is to ensure that the creation of a uniform liability regime is implemented in the most efficient and fair manner possible, without prejudicing the uniformity, integrity and effectiveness of the common rules of union law and without creating an excessive disparity in the treatment of pollution victims and the shipping industry.
‒ i voted in favour, taking into account the importance of ensuring that the uniformity, integrity and effectiveness of the eu's common rules are not adversely affected by the international commitments made by ratification or accession to the 2010 hns convention. it aims to ensure that the possibility of divergence between the dra and the 2010 hns convention is minimised and also to ensure that the permanent coexistence of two maritime liability regimes (one at union level and the other at international level) is eliminated, which would lead in particular to the fragmentation of union legislation. moreover, it would clearly undermine the determination of liability and could lead to lengthy and costly legal proceedings to the detriment of the victims and the shipping industry. in this context, it should be ensured that member states are required to take all necessary measures to achieve a concrete result, namely to ratify or accede to the 2010 hns convention within a reasonable period of time, which should not exceed two years from the date of entry into force of the council decision.

‒ tunisia is currently experiencing major difficulties. it has been repeatedly targeted by bombings and terrorist attacks that have affected key economic sectors in the country, such as tourism. growth, which was projected to be 3% in 2015, was revised down to 0.5% in 2016 and the average unemployment rate is 15%, with 20% for women and 28.6% for young graduates. in addition, the regional security context is volatile, in particular because of the country's border with libya. in august 2015, the european commission provided a second macro-financial assistance programme for tunisia, totalling eur 500 million, to be provided in the form of medium-term loans on the financial markets. this report states that the 'assistance programme will support the reforms undertaken by tunisia to improve its budgetary situation, balance of payments and create a more favourable investment climate'. the principle of cooperation and genuine development aid, which must be developed further, in respect for the sovereign will and choices of each state, is not in question. however, this type of assistance is typically accompanied by demands for 'structural and macroeconomic reforms', which we reject. for the record, our vote is against.
